title: Bartolomé de las Casas (1484–1566)
hookLine: a colonist and slaveholder who converted and spent fifty years defending Indigenous peoples

lines: A PRIEST WITH LAND AND LABORERS.
cards: A priest on the island of Cuba sits down to write a sermon for Pentecost. He owns land, and Indigenous people work it for him under a colonial grant called an encomienda.

By his own later account, he is as busy with his mines and fields as anyone. He opens the book of Ecclesiasticus for his text, and a few lines stop him cold. Years later he wrote the whole scene down himself.

teach.b: First, the lines. In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiasticus says: "The bread of the needy is the life of the poor: he that defraudeth them thereof is a man of blood."
Las Casas read that and saw his own fields: the needy were working them, and their bread was going to him.

teach.h: A FRIAR HAD ALREADY WARNED HIM.
teach.b: Second, what he had already heard. In his History of the Indies he admits that a Dominican friar had once refused him absolution for holding Indigenous people in his service, and that he had argued back.
The words hadn't landed then. Now they did. Third, what he did.

teach.h: HE GAVE THEM UP, AND SAID SO.
teach.b: He gave up the people granted to him and went to the governor to say so. Then he preached it from the pulpit: holding the islanders this way put his neighbors' souls in danger.
The neighbors, he says, were astonished, and some thought him foolish.
He crossed the ocean to argue before the court of Spain, later joined the Dominicans himself, and wrote a short and furious account of the destruction of the Indies.

teach.h: HE CHANGED AGAIN, AND ADMITTED IT.
teach.b: Fourth, the part that makes him trustworthy: he changed more than once. At one stage he had suggested bringing enslaved Africans to do the work, to spare the Indigenous people.
Later, in his History, he wrote that he regretted it, because the same injustice was being done to them. The words in Ecclesiasticus never changed. What changed was the reader.

how: Las Casas is not a canonized saint; Catholics remember him as a Dominican friar and bishop who defended Indigenous peoples, and a cause for his beatification has been opened.

o: a governor who handed out land grants in the Indies
a priest who became a defender of Indigenous peoples
a Spanish captain who conquered the island of Cuba

games.q: the man who changed — tap the pairs.

s: Las Casas never held Indigenous laborers himself
he did, under a colonial grant, until a passage in Ecclesiasticus stopped him.
he later regretted suggesting that enslaved Africans be brought to do the work
in his History he wrote that the same injustice was being done to them.
by his account they were astonished, and some thought him foolish.

games.q: you're a priest in Cuba with land and laborers. preparing a sermon, you read that whoever takes the bread of the needy is a man of blood. what do you do?
o: give up the laborers and say so publicly.
pick a different text for the sermon.
keep them, but treat them more kindly.
games.why: Las Casas gave them up, told the governor, and preached it from the pulpit, though his neighbors thought him foolish.

practice: Think of one thing you've always done, bought, said or believed without looking at who pays for it; it doesn't need to be large.
Look at it honestly, the way Las Casas looked at his fields, and ask who the needy are in that picture. If you pray, ask for the courage to change; if you don't, simply let yourself consider it.

wordCard.voice: Las Casas. A priest who held Indigenous laborers, read a line about the bread of the needy, gave them up, and spent his life defending their peoples. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: he changed. Even his own mistake, he named in writing. See you tomorrow.
